name: Octavia E. Butler Landing
summary: Perseverance touched down here on 18 February 2021. NASA later named the site after science-fiction author Octavia E. Butler.
whyItMatters: Every position in this simulator is measured from this point. The first rover waypoint in NASA's traverse data sits here.
geologicalContext: Dark, fractured crater-floor rock partly covered by sand and dust, about 2 km south-east of the western delta front.
missionRelation: Start of surface operations and of the rover checkout period.

evidence.text: Landing position 18.4446 N, 77.4509 E at about -2570 m, from NASA's rover waypoint data.

name: Why Jezero: the lake and its delta
summary: From orbit, Jezero shows two inlet valleys, one outlet valley and a fan-shaped deposit at the mouth of the western inlet. That combination means the crater once held a lake that filled until it overflowed.
whyItMatters: Deltas bury fine sediment quickly. On Earth that is where organic matter and signs of microbial life are most often preserved, which is why this site was chosen for sample collection.
geologicalContext: The crater is about 45 km wide. Orbital spectroscopy mapped clay and carbonate minerals in the fan and along the inner crater margin.
missionRelation: The delta front is the cliff line on the north-west horizon in the landing panorama.

evidence.text: Inlet and outlet valleys and the fan deposit are mapped from orbit; rover images confirmed delta-style layering in the scarps.
The lake was open (overflowing) for part of its history, with the level later falling.
How long the lake lasted and whether anything lived in it.

name: Roubion: the first coring attempt
summary: Perseverance's first attempt to drill a core, in August 2021. The rock crumbled to powder during drilling and the sealed tube held no rock, only Martian atmosphere.
whyItMatters: The tube became the mission's atmospheric sample, and the failure showed that these paver-like rocks were heavily weathered and weak.
geologicalContext: Low, polygonally fractured rocks of the crater-floor unit the team named Máaz.
missionRelation: First sampling attempt of the Crater Floor Campaign.

evidence.text: The tube was sealed without a rock core.
The rock was too altered and friable to survive coring.

name: Rochette: first rock cores
summary: The first two rock cores of the mission, Montdenier and Montagnac, were drilled from this block on the Citadelle ridge in September 2021.
whyItMatters: The rock is igneous, so its crystals can be dated in a laboratory. That would pin an absolute age onto Jezero's floor and help calibrate crater-count ages for the whole planet.
geologicalContext: Basaltic lava-like rock of the Máaz formation containing salts, which shows water moved through it after it formed.
missionRelation: Crater Floor Campaign; the cores are a pair, one kept on the rover and one later placed at Three Forks.

evidence.text: Basaltic composition and salt minerals measured by the rover's instruments.
The crater floor here is made of lava flows or similar igneous rock rather than lake sediment, which surprised many who expected sedimentary rock.
The absolute age, which needs the samples on Earth.

name: Brac outcrop: olivine cumulate
summary: Layered rock in South Séítah packed with millimetre-size olivine crystals. Cores Salette and Coulettes were drilled here.
whyItMatters: The texture shows the rock formed when olivine crystals settled in a slowly cooling body of magma, so it is igneous rather than sedimentary. Carbonate and other alteration minerals show it later reacted with water.
geologicalContext: Séítah formation, which lies beneath the Máaz rocks seen at Rochette and is therefore older.
missionRelation: Science target of the Séítah excursion (about sols 200-340).

evidence.text: Coarse olivine with pyroxene between the grains, measured by PIXL and SuperCam.
An olivine cumulate from a thick lava flow, lava lake or intrusion.
It may be part of the regional olivine-carbonate unit seen from orbit around Nili Fossae.

name: Issole: altered olivine rock
summary: Second sampled outcrop in Séítah (cores Robine and Malay). During sampling here, pebbles fell into the bit carousel and had to be cleared before the rover could continue.
whyItMatters: Together with Brac it gives two looks at the same olivine-rich unit with different amounts of water alteration.
geologicalContext: Séítah formation; SHERLOC also reported organic molecules associated with minerals in crater-floor rocks.
missionRelation: Last sampling stop before the rover drove back out of Séítah.

evidence.text: Fluorescence and Raman signals consistent with organic molecules were detected in crater-floor rocks.
Organic molecules can be made without biology (for example by water-rock reactions or delivered by meteorites); their presence is not evidence of life.

name: Sid: the Ch'ał member
summary: A boulder-like rock near the landing site, cored twice (Ha'ahóni and Atsá) in March 2022 just before the rover left the crater floor.
whyItMatters: It is thought to be the highest, and so youngest, lava unit sampled on the crater floor. Dating it and Rochette would bracket how long the floor took to form.
geologicalContext: Ch'ał member of the Máaz formation: blocky, crater-retaining rock.
missionRelation: Final cores of the Crater Floor Campaign, followed by the fast drive north around Séítah to the delta.

evidence.text: Two cores collected and sealed.
Stratigraphically the youngest crater-floor igneous unit sampled.

name: Skinner Ridge sandstone
summary: The first sedimentary rock cores of the mission (Swift Run and Skyland), drilled in July 2022 from a sandstone ledge at the base of the delta.
whyItMatters: The sand grains were carried in by the river from outside the crater, so one core holds fragments of many different source rocks from the watershed.
geologicalContext: Lower delta-front strata in the area the team called Hawksbill Gap.

evidence.text: Clastic sedimentary rock with grains of varied composition.
Deposited by flowing water entering the lake.

name: Wildcat Ridge mudstone
summary: A fine-grained, sulfate-bearing mudstone about a metre across. Cores Hazeltop and Bearwallow were taken here, and SHERLOC recorded the strongest organic-molecule signals of the mission up to that point.
whyItMatters: Fine mud that settled in salty, evaporating lake water is the kind of setting that preserves organic matter and, on Earth, fossil microbes.
geologicalContext: Delta-front lake deposits, lying low in the sedimentary stack.
missionRelation: Delta Front Campaign; one of the highest-priority samples for return to Earth.

evidence.text: Organic molecules co-located with sulfate minerals were detected by SHERLOC.
The rock formed as mud and salts settled in a lake that was evaporating.
Whether the organics have a biological origin. That cannot be decided with rover instruments.

name: Amalik outcrop at Enchanted Lake
summary: Fine-grained rock at the very base of the delta scarp at Cape Nukshak. Cores Shuyak and Mageik were drilled here.
whyItMatters: These are among the lowest, and so earliest, lake-related layers the rover reached.
geologicalContext: Base of the delta front where it meets the crater floor.
missionRelation: Delta Front Campaign; Enchanted Lake was the rover's first close look at the delta in April 2022 and it returned here months later to sample.

evidence.text: Two cores collected.
Deposited in quiet water early in the lake's history.

name: Three Forks sample depot
summary: Between 21 December 2022 and 28 January 2023 the rover set ten sealed titanium tubes on the ground here in a zigzag pattern, each a few metres from the next.
whyItMatters: The depot is a backup set. Each tube is the twin of a sample still on the rover, so a return mission would have something to collect even if the rover could not deliver its own.
geologicalContext: A flat, rock-poor patch of crater floor just in front of the delta, chosen because it is a safe place to land and drive.
missionRelation: Marks the end of the prime mission's first sampling phase. Tube positions were mapped to within about a centimetre.

evidence.text: Ten tubes: igneous and sedimentary cores, one regolith sample, one atmosphere sample and one witness tube.
When and how the samples will be brought to Earth. Mars Sample Return plans were still under review when this text was written.

name: Belva crater
summary: An impact crater roughly 0.9 km wide punched into the top of the delta. Its walls act as a natural road-cut into the fan's interior.
whyItMatters: Steeply dipping beds seen in the walls are a cross-section through sediment the river laid down, letting geologists read flow direction and energy.
geologicalContext: Upper fan. The impact happened after the delta formed.

evidence.text: Layered, inclined bedding is exposed in the crater walls.
Some of the layering may record large sandbars in a deep, fast river.

name: Fan-top boulder field
summary: The top of the fan is strewn with rounded boulders, some more than a metre across, sitting above finer layered rock.
whyItMatters: Rounded boulders that large cannot be moved by a gentle river. They point to late, powerful floods, and they are free samples of rocks from far outside the crater.
geologicalContext: Uppermost fan deposits near Snowdrift Peak.

evidence.text: Boulder-bearing conglomerate layers cap the delta.
They were laid down by episodic high-energy floods after the calmer delta-building phase.

name: Margin unit carbonates
summary: A band of carbonate-rich rock that hugs the inside of the crater rim. Several cores were collected along it.
whyItMatters: Carbonates form when water, rock and carbon dioxide react. They lock away atmosphere and, on Earth, lake-shore carbonates readily preserve signs of microbes.
geologicalContext: Mapped from orbit before landing as strong carbonate signatures along the western crater margin.

evidence.text: Abundant carbonate and silica in the sampled rocks.
Two origins are debated: carbonate precipitated along the ancient lake shore, or igneous olivine-rich rock altered in place by groundwater.

name: Cheyava Falls rock
summary: A reddish, arrowhead-shaped mudstone crossed by white calcium-sulfate veins and dotted with millimetre 'leopard spots': pale patches with dark rims containing iron and phosphate. The core taken here is named Sapphire Canyon.
whyItMatters: The rock contains organic carbon, and the spots look like the product of chemical reactions that, on Earth, are often driven by microbes. The science team has described it as a potential biosignature.
geologicalContext: Bright Angel formation, light-toned mudstone exposed on the edge of the Neretva Vallis river channel.
missionRelation: Reached in June 2024 after the rover drove along the channel floor; sampled in July 2024.

evidence.text: Organic carbon, iron-phosphate and iron-sulfide minerals arranged in reaction-front patterns.
Microbial metabolism could have produced these mineral patterns.
Non-biological chemistry could also have produced them; this has not been ruled out.
Which explanation is right. This is not a detection of life, and deciding it is expected to need the sample in laboratories on Earth.

name: Crater rim crest at Lookout Hill
summary: In December 2024, after a climb of several hundred metres over about three and a half months, the rover reached the top of Jezero's western rim.
whyItMatters: Rim rocks were heaved up from deep in the crust by the impact that made Jezero, so they are older than anything on the crater floor and unrelated to the lake.
geologicalContext: Uplifted and shattered ancient crust; the highest rover waypoint in the bundled data is here at about -1786 m.
missionRelation: Start of the Northern Rim Campaign.

evidence.text: Rover waypoint elevations rise from about -2350 m at Bright Angel to about -1786 m at the crest.
Rim blocks sample Noachian-age crust predating the crater.

name: Silver Mountain core at Shallow Bay
summary: The first core collected on the crater rim, taken in early 2025 on the slopes the team called Witch Hazel Hill.
whyItMatters: NASA described it as a one-of-a-kind sample of very old, deep crustal rock, unlike any of the cores from the crater interior.
geologicalContext: Layered and fragmented rocks exposed on the outer slope of the rim.

evidence.text: Core collected and sealed.
Likely among the oldest rocks sampled by the mission; an absolute age needs the sample on Earth.

name: Falbreen geologic contact
summary: In the Falbreen mosaic a line runs across the scene where lighter rock meets darker rock. That line is the contact between two geologic units.
whyItMatters: Contacts show which unit was laid down first, which is how a relative timeline is built without laboratory dates.
geologicalContext: Krokodillen plateau area on the outer rim. NASA described the lighter unit as olivine-rich and the darker one as clay-bearing and possibly older.
missionRelation: Imaged on sol 1516 (26 May 2025) under unusually dust-free skies.

evidence.text: A tonal boundary between two rock units is visible in the mosaic.
The clay-bearing rocks may be among the oldest terrain the rover has explored.

name: Crocodile Bridge: gateway to Lac de Charmes
summary: The rover spent the 2025/2026 solar conjunction here and built a 980-image panorama. NASA describes the spot as the transition into a region nicknamed Lac de Charmes, beyond the crater rim.
whyItMatters: The plains outside Jezero were never covered by the lake or delta, so their rocks may preserve an older chapter of Mars' crust.
missionRelation: Northern Rim Campaign; the rover then pushed farther west to Arathusa and Arbot in early 2026.

evidence.text: Panorama acquired on sol 1717 with nine frames re-taken on sol 1754.
Rocks here may record how Mars' early crust formed.
Results from Lac de Charmes were still coming in when this text was written.
